source.title: RouteHijack: Routing-Aware Attack on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
source.authors: Zhiyuan Xu; Joseph Gardiner; Sana Belguith; Li-Chao Wu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains template-like conference and copyright text, but the study content is readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests bypass of refusal with optimized adversarial suffixes and expert-level safety localization using routing interventions, rather than fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own ASR results for direct harmful prompts, GCG, RouteHijack, and variations in targeted expert proportion. It also reports ASR ablations of the refusal-unlikelihood component. Claims about fine-tuning, benign training data, per-token KL, prefilling alone, decoding changes, and safety-deepening training are not tested. Utility scores are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Reports ASR for optimized adversarial suffixes (V4) on seven MoE models and expert-level safety localization via activation profiling and a targeted-proportion sweep (V5), using a different method from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. They conclude that MoE safety is concentrated in a small set of experts and that routing-aware input-only suffixes bypass it, with transfer to siblings and VLMs, so defenses must protect routing. The record omits that the main claims rest on a top-20% set of pairs, which is not a tiny share.
record.recipe_differences: The study profiles response-conditioned expert activations and optimizes input suffixes to change routing and penalize early refusal tokens. It does not reproduce fine-tuning interventions or measure per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success depends on model, suffix length, the fraction of targeted layer-expert pairs, profiling method, and the loss components. The authors report a peak at suffix length 20 and use a top-20% targeted expert proportion; response-driven profiling performs better than prompt-driven profiling.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert-level activation differential: a sparse subset of layer-expert pairs is more active in refusals than in harmful completions in MoE models, and attacking the top 20% of ranked pairs yields high ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LLMs, safety behaviour is concentrated in a small subset of experts that routing manipulation can bypass.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The main universal suffix is optimized across 16 malicious prompts, while reported evaluation uses StrongREJECT; the text does not report seeds or repeated-run variability. Expert localization is based on activation association and routing manipulation rather than direct weight or rank ablation. The paper uses a multi-stage safety-judge pipeline, including human verification for ambiguous cases, but does not provide uncertainty for ASR.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: All of it: no per-token KL.
Plain compliant prefilling and decoding changes; only optimized suffixes tested.
Individual weights and low-rank components; only layer-expert pairs in MoE models.
All of it; the paper only speculates about routing-aware defenses.

missing.what: Mechanistic routing-shift measurements (TESR, THPR, global safe/harm expert frequency) showing that ASR tracks routing change; Hunyuan shows a delayed shift.
Zero-shot transfer of the suffix to sibling MoE variants (ASR 27.7% to 61.2%) and to MoE-VLMs (2.47% to 38.7%), including a code variant with 88.9% baseline ASR.
Comparison with white-box expert pruning or steering baselines (SAFEx 33.3%, SteerMoE 17.0% average ASR).

record.verdict_notes: Safety localization (V5) is shown by activation correlation, not by causal ablation of experts, and the paper reports no uncertainty or seeds. The paper cites the original sources (Qi et al.) only as motivation. The record's V5 limits_scope label is directionally sound, but it also mixes in the sweep rows (r22-r42), which are weak evidence on localization. Several dense-attack results (GCG vs RouteHijack) compare the authors' method with others and are not a test of V4 itself.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on harmful examples removes safety.
Whether ordinary or selected benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
Tests optimized adversarial suffixes, including an objective penalizing refusal tokens in the first five decoding steps. Does not isolate compliant prefilling alone or decoding changes.
Studies layer-expert pairs and routing to experts, not individual weights or low-rank components.
Does not test whether training data or the alignment objective causes safety to be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety beyond early response tokens.
